newsitem.title: UK: Crude oil tanker rates seen rising in 1997-analyst.
newsitem.headline: Crude oil tanker rates seen rising in 1997-analyst.

text.p: The crude oil tanker market enters 1997 in a quietly bullish mood, encouraged by growing world oil demand and prospects of a stable or contracting very large crude carrier (VLCC) fleet.
"Rates on average have already picked up since 1995 as a result of improving fundamentals and an increased demand," said Drewry Shipping Consultants in a report on VLCCs in 1997-98.
"This upward trend can be expected to be maintained, although (it may) show more volatility throughout the period."

Drewry said relatively high anticipated VLCC scrappings over the next two years could lead to a contracting fleet or only a marginal increase "whilst demand is expected to be driven further on the basis of improving fundamentals."
Oslo-based Intertanko, which represents almost 80 percent of the world independent tanker owners, is also quietly confident about prospects for 1997.
"Owners are expecting improved rates even if supply and demand is fairly flat," said Erik Ranheim, head of Intertanko's market research and statistics department.
"That is what happened (in 1996) and we hope and believe it will happen in 1997."
Ranheim said he expected regionalisation of trade to continue as consumers seek oil closer to home.

"Rates have increased by about 20 percent for big ships this year, and big ships are going increasingly for shorter haul voyages," he added, noting rising European dependence on North Sea oil and the U.S. importing more from Latin America and Canada.
Analysts said buoyant world oil demand would boost the tanker market, with the International Energy Agency forecasting a 1.9 million barrels per day increase this year over 1996.

"Average earnings were up 15-20 percent in 1996 from 1995 and that should continue," said a London analyst who asked not to be identified. "There have been gains in rates and owners have been adept at keeping costs under control."
Mark Jenkins, head of research at London brokers Simpson Spence & Young (SS&Y), was "reasonably positive for 1997."
"There is evidence that quality tonnage is starting to command preferential rates and recognition from charterers...
"The Japanese and South Koreans are very much leading this drive and the major oil companies are generally becoming more demanding," he added.
A further bullish factor is the recent limited return of Iraq to the world oil market after six years of U.N. sanctions.

London-based Maritime Strategies International (MSI) said the limited resumption of Iraqi exports under a U.N. oil for food deal "will, at least in the short term, provide a stimulant to the tanker market by increasing the volumes of oil on the water."

MSI said they saw signs of million-barrel (Suezmax) liftings picking up in the North Sea after a dip in December, and they anticipate that "earnings will be maintained above $20,000 per day over the next six months" against an average of $19,800 in 1996.

But they also issued a note of caution, saying, "Suezmaxes have been the most consistent performer in the tanker market in 1996 and MSI anticipate that, with owner confidence high, this sector is vulnerable to over-ordering during the next six months."

On smaller, 80,000-tonne vessels, MSI are also optimistic, seeing average earnings of up to $18,000 per day over the next six months, against $17,200 in 1996. They said a "strong pick up" in such cargoes seems inevitable, given sharp rises forecast for non-OPEC oil output.
SS&Y's Jenkins said a sharp fall in rates in most sectors in late 1996 "is not an automatic indicator of worse things to come in 1997" as such a fall frequently occurred at the end of the year.
But another analyst put considerable stress on the year-end weakness.

Jarle Hammer of Oslo-based Fearnleys said that despite growth in world oil demand of almost three percent in 1996 and a rise in the tanker fleet of only one percent, "as the year elapsed, crude tanker rates were again down to dismal levels" compared with bullish summer rates.

In his December report, Hammer noted the increased competition oil is now facing from gas and coal and added: "Against this background, I would not be very surprised to see a less favourable -- albeit still maybe rather decent -- tanker market ahead of us than expected by many others."
